al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-ix:
The ninth tome of Les Prairies d'Or, printed in 1877, completes Barbier de Meynard's French al-Masudi. The Muruj al-Dhahab of al-Masudi, the Meadows of Gold, is the work of a tenth-century Baghdad scholar who traveled to India, Persia, and East Africa. With this tome the Société Asiatique set stands whole.

Al-Masudi aimed at nothing less than the whole known world. He covers its lands and seas, its ancient kings, and its faiths. The annals of Islam run down to his own time. His method mixes chronicle, geography, and the tales of the road. The French version remains the fullest form of his book in a Western tongue. The long labor of the editors ends here.
australia-felix:
Henry Handel Richardson, pen name of writer Ethel Robertson, opened her Richard Mahony story with Australia Felix on the Victorian goldfields. A proem buries a digger in a collapsed shaft on the Gravel Pits, while his mate Long Jim weeps for his luck. Richardson builds the novel from her father's life as a goldfields doctor. Fortune will smile and ruin by turns.

Richard Mahony, an English doctor, throws up medicine for digging and trade in Ballarat. Fever lifts and drops him as claims fail, flood, and pay out without pattern. Marriage to Mary Turnham brings steadiness he cannot keep, and pride wounds his chances. Stores, shares, and starts cycle through the town's boom years. Richardson writes the fields with mud, water, and failure in detail. Readers of classics start the Mahony trilogy here, where a man's hunger for fortune shows the flaw that dogs him through later volumes.
beatrix:
Honore de Balzac's Beatrix, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley, carries a note admitting what Balzac usually escaped: readers recognized real persons in this novel. The Marquise de Rochefide, Beatrix, was drawn from Marie d'Agoult, and Camille Maupin, the woman writer in the tale, from George Sand. The Breton setting at Guerande frames their rivalry.

Calyste du Guenic, a noble Breton youth, loves Beatrix, who plays with his devotion while Camille, older and wiser, studies him and forgives much. A letter in the middle weighs whether women sure of being loved pardon a passing infidelity as a triumph. Balzac turns a society scandal into a study of youth, genius, and manipulation.
blix:
Frank Norris published Blix in 1899, a short San Francisco love story named for its heroine, Travis Bessemer, called Blix. She lives with her family in a flat on the Washington Street hill, above a famous view of the bay. Young writer Condy Rivers courts her through long talks, walks, and shared jokes.

Norris keeps the plot light: fishing trips, a Chinese restaurant, newspaper work, and Blix's blunt refusal to be merely decorative. She counts out her own savings to help Condy, and the two test whether affection can survive ambition and separation. The novel shows Norris's softer side, far from his later tales of wheat and greed, and preserves a vivid picture of 1890s San Francisco.
boy-scouts-in-the-coal-caverns-or-the-li:
Boy Scouts in the Coal Caverns, or The Light in Tunnel Six, is credited on its title page to Major Archibald Lee Fletcher. The story opens in the dusky office of the idle Labyrinth mine. Case Canfield, the caretaker, addresses four lads of seventeen in scout khaki. Give me a good husky band of Boy Scouts, he says. They will do the job if it can be done.

The four are the Beaver Patrol of Chicago. Will Smith is Scoutmaster and George Benton Patrol Leader. Sandy Green and Tommy Gregory complete the party. Their sleeve medals show examinations passed as ambulance aids, stalkers, pioneers, and seamen. A Chicago criminal lawyer has sent them to the deserted mine. Its veins have not given out, Canfield hints. Something else closed it. Fletcher's series sends scouts wherever danger keeps a secret, and a coal mine keeps several.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aix:
Aix, Aquae Sextiae, in full the Archdiocese of Aix, Arles, and Embrun, covers Aix and Arles districts in the Bouches-du-Rhone. Before the Revolution, Aix's archdiocese counted Apt, Riez, Frejus, Gap, and Sisteron as suffragans. Today Arles and Embrun no longer exist as archbishoprics, and Aix has Marseille, Frejus, Digne, Gap, Ajaccio, and Nice as dependents.

Tradition makes St. Maximinus, one of the seventy-two disciples and Mary Magdalen's companion, the first Bishop of Aix. Duchesne seems to have proved this saint was not Aix's first bishop, nor linked to Mary Magdalen except in recent legends devised about the mid-eleventh century by Vezelay monks. The first historically known bishop is Lazarus, about the beginning of the fifth century. Only late in the eighth century did Aix become an archbishopric, having depended until then on Arles. In 1905 the archdiocese had 188,872 inhabitants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-crucifi:
The altar crucifix is the altar's principal ornament, set there to recall that the Victim offered on the altar matches the one on the Cross. It must stand on the altar whenever Mass is celebrated, at the middle between the candlesticks, large enough for celebrant and people to see conveniently. Benedict XIV's constitution Accepimus of 16 July 1746 fixed the requirement.

Two exceptions allow the regular crucifix to stay. One is when the Crucifixion itself is the altarpiece's principal part. The other is when the Blessed Sacrament is exposed, following local custom. A saint merely holding a crucifix in a picture does not count as the first case. From Passion Sunday's first Vespers to the Good Friday unveiling, the altar crucifix wears a violet veil, white on Holy Thursday and black permitted on Good Friday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archaeology-o:
The Archaeology of the Cross and Crucifix traces the sign of the cross from a primitive mark long predating Christianity to the Christian crucifix, the cross bearing Christ's body. In simplest form, two lines crossing at right angles, the sign appears in East and West from remote antiquity, and some have claimed ethnographic importance for its spread. Though pleasing as decoration, it was from the earliest times not mere ornament but a symbol with religious meaning.

Its primitive form seems to have been the gamma cross, better known by its Sanskrit name swastika. Later it was curved at the ends or enriched with lines and points meeting at the centre. From those early signs the long article follows the cross into Christian art, worship, and devotion, showing how a universal mark became the central emblem of a faith. It also shows how the bare cross grew into the crucifix.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beatrix:
Beatrix is a name borne by several holy women, none of very eminent renown. The Roman virgin and martyr Beatrix, inscribed on 29 July, is believed sister to martyrs Simplicius and Faustinus, whom she buried. Legend says her betrothed Lucretius denounced her as Christian, and her own servants strangled her. Beatrix d'Este, who died in 1262, lost her betrothed Galeazzo Manfredi to battle wounds just before their wedding.

Refusing to return home, she served God under the Benedictine rule at San Lazzaro outside Ferrara, her festival kept on 19 January. Another Beatrix, the Bohemian Bozena, became a nun and was honored on 13 November as St Hrosnata's sister. A later Beatrix, honored by Queen Isabel the Catholic, founded an order for the Immaculate Conception, approved in 1480, but died ten days before its inauguration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-celestin-jose:
Célestin Joseph Félix was a French Jesuit born at Neuville-sur-l'Escaut on 28 June 1810 and dying at Lille on 7 July 1891. After studies at Cambrai and a spell teaching rhetoric, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1837, studied at Louvain, and was ordained in 1842. His early Lenten sermons, above all one on true patriotism preached at Ath, won him a brilliant name for eloquence.

Called to Paris, he preached at St. Thomas d'Aquin, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and Saint-Sulpice. From 1853 to 1870 he held the pulpit of Notre-Dame, succeeding Lacordaire and de Ravignan. Critics found him short on imagination and on Lacordaire's fire, but stronger in dialectic and surer in doctrine, with a richer diction than de Ravignan's and more originality than Monsabré's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-de-la:
Charles de la Croix was a missionary born at Hoorbeke-St-Corneille in Belgium in 1792 and dead at Ghent in 1869. At Ghent seminary he resisted Napoleon's imposed bishop with fellow students. He and his brother Joseph were jailed at Wesel, where Joseph died. After the Empire fell he resumed his studies. Ordained by Bishop Dubourg of Louisiana, he followed him to the United States with seminarians and Flemish workmen.

In May 1818 he was sent to Barrens, Missouri, to oversee a new seminary for the Louisiana diocese. That December he moved to Florissant, near St. Louis. Helped by the Religious of the Sacred Heart, he laboured among Catholic families and Osage Indians, preparing the way for De Smet's Jesuits in 1823. When Van Quickenborne arrived with eight Belgian companions, de la Croix had nearly finished and paid for a brick church. He returned to Belgium in 1833, a canon of Ghent cathedral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-vic: This 1913 reference piece on Delacroix — the romantic master. Henry Anger honors his famous canvases. His brush fired the July salon. Paris hailed its impetuous genius. The Rubens of the nineteenth century. His 1830 Liberty is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-xavi: A 1913 entry on Charlevoix — the Jesuit of New France. Edward Spillane honors his famous Histoire. His pen chronicled the Canadian missions. The order prized its learned son. The historian of the French colonies. His 1761 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guadix: This 1913 reference piece on Guadix — the Andalusian diocese. Ramón Ruiz Amadó gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the southern flock. The alcazaba crowns the old town. A see of the Spanish south. Its 4th-century see is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leo-ix: A 1913 entry on Leo IX — the reforming pope. Horace Mann honors his famous synods. His zeal cleansed the Roman Church. The age hailed the holy name. The eleventh century knew his sway. His 1054 death is famed. His 1049 synods are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-dominiq: A 1913 entry on Bouix — the Jesuit canonist. John Creagh honors his famous works. His pen ordered the Church's law. The order prized its learned son. The jurists cite his name. His 1870 death is famed. His 1870 works are famed. His 1870 canonical tomes are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-minucius-feli: A 1913 entry on Minucius Felix — the Latin apologist. Paul Lejay honors his famous Octavius. His pen defended the Christian name. The fathers prized the polished page. The third century knew his toil. His 250 death is famed. His Octavius is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-raffei: This biographical entry profiles Pierre Raffeix, a French Jesuit of the 1600s, tracing his career, his writings, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Jesuit gallery, preserved among its learned 17th-century missionaries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-benedict: Benedict IX was the scandalous boy-pope who sold the tiara. This entry traces his three pontificates, his simony, and his infamy. The most disgraced of all popes: his shameful fall sparked the great Gregorian reform movement of the whole Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-boniface: Boniface IX was the pope of the Roman obedience during the Great Schism. This entry traces his pontificate, his finances, and his long war. The pope of the divided Church: his heavy taxes funded the long schism's war in Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-clement-: Clement IX was the Rospigliosi pope of the late 1660s, patron of Bernini's angels. This entry notes his brief pontificate and his works. The pope of the Ponte Sant'Angelo: his brief reign blessed the Roman arts generously and well indeed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gregory-: Gregory IX was the pope who excommunicated Frederick II and organized the Inquisition. This entry traces his pontificate, his wars, and his decretals. The foe of the Stupor Mundi: his great decretals ordered the Church's law for centuries afterward in force.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-innocent: Innocent IX was the pope of two months in 1591. This entry notes his brief pontificate and the scant records as the 1913 editors found them. A shadow of the Counter-Reformation: his few weeks left no mark on history's page.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-ix: John IX was the pope who rehabilitated Formosus and condemned the Cadaver Synod. This entry traces his pontificate, his synods, and his justice. The restorer of the wronged dead: his just synods annulled the ghastly outrage of 897's corpse synod.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xvi: This entry untangles the numbering confusion between John XVIII and John XIX. A specialized study of papal chronology as the 1913 editors recorded it, clarifying the medieval miscounts for the puzzled modern reader at very long last indeed in print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-pius-ix: Pius IX was the longest-reigning pope, of Vatican I and the Syllabus. This long entry traces his pontificate, his dogmas, and his captivity. Pio Nono, the pope of the century: his Marian dogma defined the Catholic age of 1854's December.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-stephen-: Stephen VIII was the pope of the mid-930s who faced the Roman nobles. This entry notes his pontificate and the scant records as the 1913 editors found them. A quiet name of the iron century: his months left no mark.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-louis-ix: St. Louis IX was the king of France. This very long entry examines his crusades, his Sainte-Chapelle, and his fame. The most Christian of the medieval kings: his holy crown sealed Paris in the 1240s' Sainte-Chapelle in the palace of the Cité.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-nabor-and: Nabor and Felix were the martyrs of Milan. This entry traces their Mauritania, their Maximian, and their crowns. The soldiers of the African legion: their martyr's blood sealed Lodi in the 303 of the Maximian in the town of the Adda.
doe-osti-3022112-report-on-inventory-of-: BOR-60 got inventory-reported, and this DOE text counts six capsule samples. The pages detail the findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The capsules were six. The data were nuclear. The BOR-60 was samples. The capsules were inventory. The six were report.
doe-osti-3066504-demonstration-of-grid-s: Wheatridge got grid-services-demonstrated, and this DOE text mixes forming and following. The pages detail the renewable findings. The grid folks get their data. The technologies were grid. The data were grid. The following were grid. The renewable were findings.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-appen:
Thomas Carlyle's appendix to his Friedrich history prints a piece translated sixteen years earlier, some years before any part of the history itself was written, as his headnote explains. The intercalated commentary dates from the same early time and is now partly superfluous to diligent readers, he admits, but he leaves it where not compelled to change. The piece preserves his first approach to the Prussian materials.

Its dialogue scenes bring General von Ziethen, the rugged, brave old cavalryman with hanging brows and dim-fiery pious thoughts, before the king in direct speech. Readers of the whole twenty-one volumes can watch Carlyle's manner forming here: the documents quoted, hectored, and loved into narrative. The appendix is a workshop door left open.
the-danish-history-books-i-ix: Saxo Grammaticus, called Saxo the Learned, wrote his Danish History in Latin in the early years of the thirteenth century, as Douglas B. Killings's preparer's note explains. The English text rests on The Nine Books of the Danish History of Saxo Grammaticus, translated by Oliver Elton for the Norroena Society in 1905. Saxo wrote sixteen books in all, but Elton rendered only the first nine, and no public-domain English version of books ten through sixteen is known to the preparer. Only this note and a bibliography are present here.
the-devolutionist-and-the-emancipatrix:
Homer Eon Flint pairs two tales in The Devolutionist and The Emancipatrix. The first opens under the head Out of Their Minds. Mrs. Kinney leads a caller to a locked door with a warning: make no sound, no matter what he sees. She turns the key, and the two step softly into the private study of her husband, Dr. William Kinney.

The room itself is ordinary enough, with book shelves, cases of surgical and psychological instruments, star charts, maps, and astronomical apparatus. Its four chairs are not. Each holds a human being, and none of the four stirs as the pair enters. The doctor sits half reclined, gray head resting wearily on one shoulder. Mrs. Kinney whispers the names: Mr. Smith beside him, and opposite, Mr. and Mrs. Van Emmon, all sunk in complete, motionless sleep.
the-emancipatrix:
Homer Eon Flint's The Emancipatrix opens in a doctor's room, where a blunt question lands: what has come between the geologist Van Emmon and his wife? Van, calm but held tight, traces it to a joint probe of Capellette two months past. Both he and Billie still trust the Venusian formula, he says, and long to visit more worlds by telepathy.

Four friends can project their minds to other planets. What they find there tests their bonds on Earth. Flint, an early pulp hand, blends space travel with close talk of marriage and trust.
the-executor-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magaz:
Mrs. Oliphant's tale The Executor ran in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume eighty-nine, covering January to June 1861. The volume's title page names William Blackwood and Sons of Edinburgh and their London house in Paternoster Row. The tale opens mid-scene: John Brown declares the woman was certainly mad, a strange speech for the place.

A grim parlour holds two decanters on a bare, shining table, blinds drawn, and half a dozen folk in mourning, their faces a mix of shock and spite. A will has just been read. Oliphant spins greed and duty from that charged room.
the-human-comedy-introductions-and-appen:
Honoré de Balzac's fiction project receives its frame in this volume. It gathers the introductions and appendix for The Human Comedy. George Saintsbury supplied an introduction and a brief biography. The appendix lists Balzac's titles in French. English translations stand beside them, grouped by his classifications. Balzac's own introduction of 1842 is reprinted. Saintsbury opens with a letter to Balzac's sister. Without genius, Balzac wrote, he was done for.

Saintsbury argues those words unlock the man. Libraries have been written about Balzac since. Few phrases sum him up so well. He had staked everything on an unproved gift. The volume suits readers moving through the novels in order. It also suits anyone who wants the author's own map. His fictional universe sorts into scenes of private, provincial, and Parisian life. Balzac invented that scheme himself.
the-sign-at-six:
Stewart Edward White's The Sign at Six carries four illustrations by M. Leone Bracker. Its contents list twenty-four chapters. The owner of New York opens the book. The shadow of mystery and the moving finger follow. Darkness and panic come at chapter four. Later headings promise a world of ghosts and the great silence. The lifting of the spell and the plague of cold also appear.

Chapter one introduces Percy Darrow in a single unfolding sentence. He is a young man of scientific training, White writes. His manners are indolent and his appearance effeminate. Hidden energy and absolute courage complete the portrait, the sentence says. There the portion shown breaks off, leaving Darrow lounging at the threshold of the mystery.
